name: The keyboard map
explanation: The keyboard repeats the same seven white-key names, C through B. The black keys come in groups of two and three — C always sits just left of a group of two.
examples: C is left of the two black keys
F is left of the three black keys

questions.promptText: Which key sits just LEFT of every group of TWO black keys?
questions.explanation: C always sits just left of the two black keys — that's the fastest way to find it anywhere.
choiceExplanations: Right — C always sits just left of every pair of black keys. It's the fastest landmark on the whole keyboard.
E sits on the other side — just RIGHT of the two black keys, not left of them.
F belongs to the other group: it sits just left of the THREE black keys.
B sits just right of the three black keys — wrong group, wrong side.

questions.promptText: Which key sits just LEFT of every group of THREE black keys?
questions.explanation: F sits just left of the three black keys.
choiceExplanations: C is the landmark for the TWO black keys — this question is about the group of three.
Right — F sits just left of every group of three black keys, exactly like C does for the pair.
G is inside the three-black-key group's white keys, not at its left edge.
A also sits within that stretch — two white keys right of F, not at the edge.

questions.promptText: How many different white-key NAMES are there before the pattern repeats?
questions.explanation: Seven names — C D E F G A B — then the pattern starts over an octave higher.
choiceExplanations: Five is the finger count in one hand position — the musical alphabet is longer.
Right — seven names, C D E F G A B, then the pattern repeats an octave higher.
Ten would overshoot: after G the names loop back to A, so only seven exist.
Twelve counts every key including the black ones — the white-key NAMES are just seven.

questions.promptText: You're on C and step UP one white key. Where are you?
questions.explanation: Stepping up from C lands on D — names go up the alphabet as you go right.
choiceExplanations: B is one step DOWN from C — the alphabet runs backward when you move left.
Right — one white key up from C is D. Names climb the alphabet as you move right.
E is two white keys up from C — that's a skip, not a step.
G is four white keys away — several steps, not one.

questions.promptText: Two keys with the same name, eight steps apart, are called…
questions.explanation: Same name, higher or lower — that distance is an octave.
choiceExplanations: A chord is several DIFFERENT notes sounding together — these two share one name.
Right — same name, eight steps apart: that distance is an octave.
A scale is the whole ladder of notes in between, not the distance itself.
A bar is a slice of TIME (beats), nothing to do with pitch distance.

questions.promptText: Higher-sounding notes live in which direction on the keyboard?
questions.explanation: Right = higher, left = lower. Your ear and the map agree.
choiceExplanations: Leftward is the low, rumbling end — the opposite direction.
Right — pitch rises to the right, always. Your ear and the keyboard map agree.
The middle is just where C4 happens to live — height keeps changing across it.
It never varies: right = higher on every piano, every time.

name: Beat, bar, and downbeat
explanation: The beat is the steady pulse you'd tap your foot to. Beats group into bars, and the first beat of each bar — the downbeat — carries a little extra weight.

questions.promptText: The steady pulse you tap your foot to is called the…
questions.explanation: That's the beat — everything else in the music lines up against it.
choiceExplanations: The melody is the tune you hum — it rides ON TOP of the pulse.
Right — the steady pulse is the beat; everything else lines up against it.
A chord is notes sounding together — harmony, not time.
A phrase is a musical 'sentence' spanning many beats.

questions.promptText: The FIRST beat of every bar is called the…
questions.explanation: Beat 1 is the downbeat — it's where the bar 'lands'.
choiceExplanations: An upbeat is the beat BEFORE the bar starts — the 'and-a' that leads in.
The backbeat is beats 2 and 4 — the clap in pop and blues, not beat 1.
Right — beat 1 is the downbeat, where the bar lands.
Offbeats are the in-between moments, the opposite of a strong beat 1.

questions.promptText: You count '1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4…'. What happens at every '1'?
questions.explanation: Each count of 1 is the start of a new bar — the downbeat.
choiceExplanations: The music keeps going — '1' is a beginning, not a stop.
Right — every count of '1' is a new bar starting: the downbeat.
Tempo stays steady; only your count resets, not the speed.
It IS special — the downbeat is the strongest landing point in the bar.

questions.promptText: If you play a wrong note, the best move for the groove is to…
choices: Keep going and land the next beat
questions.explanation: Musicians keep the pulse. Recover on the next beat — nobody hears the note you didn't replay.
choiceExplanations: Stopping breaks the one thing listeners actually track — the pulse.
Playing it late doubles the damage: now the wrong note AND the timing suffer.
Right — keep the pulse and land the next beat. Nobody hears the note you didn't replay.
Slowing down bends the groove for everyone; the beat shouldn't apologize for one note.

questions.promptText: A metronome is for practicing your…
questions.explanation: The click is an honest timing mirror — that's why the app scores timing, not just notes.
choiceExplanations: Note names live on the keyboard map — the click can't teach you those.
Right — the metronome is an honest timing mirror. That's why the app scores timing, not just notes.
Chord spelling is theory work — no click required.
Volume is touch and dynamics; the metronome only speaks in time.

name: Common time — 4/4
explanation: A time signature describes the bar: the TOP number says how many beats each bar has; the BOTTOM number says which note value counts as one beat. 4/4 — 'common time' — means four quarter-note beats per bar.

questions.promptText: In a time signature, the TOP number tells you…
questions.explanation: Top number = beats per bar. In 4/4 you count to four, then a new bar starts.
choiceExplanations: Speed is tempo (BPM) — a separate dial entirely; time signatures don't set it.
Right — the top number is beats per bar. In 4/4 you count to four, then a new bar starts.
The key comes from the key signature (sharps and flats), not the meter.
Loudness is dynamics — written with letters like p and f, not numbers.

questions.promptText: In 4/4, the BOTTOM 4 means one beat lasts a…
questions.explanation: The bottom number names the note value of the beat — 4 means quarter note.
choiceExplanations: A whole note would be a bottom '1' — it fills a whole 4/4 bar by itself.
A half note would be a bottom '2' — two of those per 4/4 bar.
Right — the bottom 4 means the quarter note owns the beat.
An eighth note would be a bottom '8', like the 8 in 6/8.

questions.promptText: A 4/4 bar so far holds three quarter notes. What single note completes it?
questions.explanation: Three beats are used, one is left — one more quarter note fills the bar.
choiceExplanations: Right — three beats used, one left: one more quarter note completes the four.
A half note is TWO beats — that would overflow the bar to five.
A whole note is four beats on its own — way too much for the one slot left.
Not yet — three quarters only cover three of the four beats.

questions.promptText: You hear: ONE-two-three-four, ONE-two-three-four. The meter is…
questions.explanation: An accent every four beats is the sound of 4/4 — common time.
choiceExplanations: 2/4 would accent every TWO counts: ONE-two, ONE-two.
3/4 would accent every THREE counts — the waltz sway.
Right — an accent every four beats is 4/4, common time.
6/8 rolls in two big lilting groups of three — a different feel altogether.

questions.promptText: How many quarter notes fit in TWO bars of 4/4?
questions.explanation: Four per bar × two bars = eight.
choiceExplanations: Four is just ONE bar's worth.
Six would be two bars of 3/4 — wrong meter.
Right — four per bar × two bars = eight.
Sixteen would be FOUR bars of 4/4, or eighth notes — twice too many.

name: Tier 1 check: keys, beats, and bars
explanation: Everything Tier 1 taught, in one short check: the keyboard map, the beat, and 4/4 time.

questions.promptText: Which key sits just left of the two black keys?
questions.explanation: C — left of every pair of black keys.
choiceExplanations: Right — C sits just left of every pair of black keys.
D sits BETWEEN the two black keys, not beside them.
F is the landmark for the THREE black keys.
G lives inside the three-black-key group — nowhere near the pair's left edge.

questions.promptText: In 4/4 time, how many beats are in each bar?
questions.explanation: Four quarter-note beats per bar.
choiceExplanations: Two beats per bar is 2/4 — march time.
Three beats per bar is 3/4 — waltz time.
Right — 4/4 means four quarter-note beats every bar.
Eight would be a very different signature (like 8/8) — the top 4 says four.

questions.promptText: The first beat of a bar is the…
questions.explanation: The downbeat — count '1'.
choiceExplanations: Offbeats are the weak in-between moments — the opposite of beat 1.
Right — beat 1 is the downbeat, counted '1'.
The backbeat is beats 2 and 4 — the clap, not the landing.
A pickup comes BEFORE the first full bar — it leads INTO the downbeat.

questions.promptText: Notes get HIGHER as you move which way?
questions.explanation: Rightward = higher pitch, always.
choiceExplanations: Left is the low end — bass territory.
Right — pitch always rises as you move right.
The middle is just middle C's neighborhood, not a direction of change.
It never depends — the keyboard's pitch map is fixed.

questions.promptText: Stepping up one white key from E lands on…
questions.explanation: E steps up to F — they're direct neighbors with no black key between.
choiceExplanations: D is a step DOWN from E.
Right — E's upstairs neighbor is F; there's no black key between them.
G is two steps up from E — a skip past F.
Stepping means moving — you can't step up and stay on E.

questions.promptText: A 4/4 bar already has two quarter notes and one half note. It is…
questions.explanation: 2 + 2 = 4 beats — the bar is complete.
choiceExplanations: Count again: 1 + 1 + 2 = 4 — nothing is missing.
The bar needs four total and has four.
Right — two quarters (2) plus a half (2) is exactly four beats: full.
It fits perfectly — four beats in a four-beat bar isn't overfull.

questions.promptText: If you miss a note mid-song, you should…
choices: Keep the pulse and catch the next beat
Play it twice to make up
questions.explanation: Keeping the pulse is the skill. Recovery beats perfection.
choiceExplanations: Restarting punishes the 99% you played fine — and breaks the pulse.
Pausing to hunt for it breaks time worse than the missed note did.
Right — keep the pulse, catch the next beat. Recovery beats perfection.
Playing it twice puts TWO notes in the wrong place instead of none.

questions.promptText: Two notes sound in a row and the second is lower. It moved…
questions.explanation: Lower sound = downward movement = leftward on the keys.
choiceExplanations: Up would mean the second note sounded HIGHER — it didn't.
Right — a lower sound is downward movement: leftward on the keys.
It clearly changed — 'nowhere' would mean the same pitch twice.
Louder is volume, not direction — a different dimension of sound.

name: The staff points the way
explanation: Notes sit on five lines and four spaces. Higher on the staff = higher on the keyboard; bar lines slice the music into bars.

questions.promptText: A melody whose notes climb UP the staff moves which way on the keyboard?
questions.explanation: Up the staff is up in pitch — rightward on the keys.
choiceExplanations: Left is LOWER — the opposite of climbing.
Right — up the staff is up in pitch, which is rightward on the keys.
The clef changes WHERE the map starts, never which way is up.
The melody moves — a climbing shape can't stand still.

questions.promptText: The vertical lines drawn through the staff are…
questions.explanation: Bar lines mark where one bar ends and the next begins.
choiceExplanations: Beats are what you count — they're felt, not drawn as lines.
Right — bar lines fence off one bar from the next.
Stems are the thin strokes attached to individual note heads.
Rests mark silence and have their own symbols — not vertical lines.

questions.promptText: Two notes on the SAME line or space of the staff are…
questions.explanation: Same position, same pitch — repeated notes sit in one spot.
choiceExplanations: A step apart would put them on NEIGHBORING positions — line to space.
Right — same line or space means the very same pitch, repeated.
An octave apart would separate them by four lines of the staff.
Two notes IN A ROW are a melody; chords stack notes at the same moment.

questions.promptText: From a line to the very next space is a…
questions.explanation: Line to neighboring space = one step (like E to F on the keys).
choiceExplanations: Right — line to its neighboring space is one step, like E to F on the keys.
A skip would jump PAST the neighboring space to the next line.
A leap is bigger still — several positions at once.
A rest is silence — no movement at all.

questions.promptText: A melody that looks like a descending staircase on the staff will SOUND…
questions.explanation: The staff is a picture of pitch: falling shapes fall in sound.
choiceExplanations: Higher and higher would LOOK like a rising staircase.
Right — the staff is a picture of pitch: falling shapes fall in sound.
Staying the same would draw a flat, level line of notes.
Louder is dynamics — the staircase shape is about pitch, not volume.

name: March time — 2/4
explanation: 2/4 has two quarter-note beats per bar: ONE-two, ONE-two. Same beat as 4/4, half the bar.

questions.promptText: How many beats fit in one bar of 2/4?
questions.explanation: The top number says two beats per bar.
choiceExplanations: Right — the top 2 promises two beats per bar.
Three per bar is 3/4 — the waltz.
Four per bar is 4/4 — common time.
Eight would need a top 8 — much longer bars than this.

questions.promptText: You hear: ONE-two, ONE-two, ONE-two. The meter is…
questions.explanation: An accent every two beats is the sound of 2/4 — a march.
choiceExplanations: Right — an accent every two beats is 2/4: march time.
3/4 would go ONE-two-three — a three-count sway.
4/4 would stretch to ONE-two-three-four.
6/8 lilts in two groups of three — a rolling compound feel.

questions.promptText: A 2/4 bar already holds one quarter note. What completes it?
questions.explanation: One beat used, one left — a single quarter note fills it.
choiceExplanations: Right — one beat used, one left: a single quarter note fills it.
A half note is two beats — the bar only has room for one more.
A whole note is four beats — twice the entire bar.
It isn't full yet — one of the two beats is still empty.

questions.promptText: Compared with 4/4, a bar of 2/4 is…
questions.explanation: Half the beats per bar — the downbeat comes around twice as often.
choiceExplanations: Twice as long would be a top number of 8 against 4 — backwards.
Right — half the beats per bar, so the downbeat comes around twice as often.
Same length would need the same beat count — 2 ≠ 4.
Speed is tempo, not meter — 2/4 says nothing about fast or slow.

questions.promptText: In 2/4, the downbeat arrives every…
choices: Bar line is not a downbeat
questions.explanation: Count 1-2, 1-2 — every second beat starts a new bar.
choiceExplanations: Every beat can't be a downbeat — only bar starts are.
Right — count 1-2, 1-2: every second beat begins a new bar.
Every four beats is 4/4's spacing, not 2/4's.
Bar lines mark exactly where downbeats land — they're tightly linked.

name: Tier 2 check: reading and meter
explanation: The staff map, bar lines, and telling 2/4 from 4/4.

questions.promptText: Up the staff means which way on the keyboard?
questions.explanation: The staff is a pitch map: up is up.
choiceExplanations: Right — the staff is a pitch map: up the staff, up the keyboard, rightward.
Left is lower — descending, not ascending.
The map never changes song to song.
It has to be one of them — pitch always moves somewhere on the keys.

questions.promptText: ONE-two, ONE-two is the feel of…
questions.explanation: Accents every two beats — march time.
choiceExplanations: Right — accents every two beats: march time, 2/4.
3/4 counts in threes — ONE-two-three.
4/4 counts in fours — twice this length.
There's clearly a repeating accent — that IS meter.

questions.promptText: ONE-two-three-four, ONE-two-three-four is the feel of…
questions.explanation: Accents every four beats — common time.
choiceExplanations: 2/4 would land its accent twice as often.
3/4 would count ONE-two-three.
Right — accents every four beats: 4/4, common time.
6/8 rolls in two big groups of three — a lilt, not a square four.

questions.promptText: Bar lines divide music into…
questions.explanation: Each bar holds the number of beats the top number promises.
choiceExplanations: Phrases are musical sentences — they can span several bars.
Right — bar lines carve the music into bars of equal beats, as the top number promises.
Chords are stacked notes — harmony, not time-slicing.
Pages are just where the paper runs out.

questions.promptText: A song starts on beat 2 with the first bar incomplete. That opening is a…
questions.explanation: A pickup (anacrusis) — the Saints starts exactly this way.
choiceExplanations: Right — an incomplete opening bar is a pickup (anacrusis). The Saints starts exactly this way.
The downbeat is beat 1 itself — this song starts BEFORE its first full one.
A rest is written silence, not a late entrance.
A coda is an ENDING section — the wrong end of the song.

questions.promptText: Notes stepping line-space-line-space on the staff are moving by…
questions.explanation: Adjacent staff positions are neighboring keys — steps.
choiceExplanations: Right — adjacent staff positions are neighboring keys: steps.
Skips would jump line-to-line or space-to-space, passing one position.
Octaves leap four lines at once — much bigger jumps.
Chords stack notes vertically — this is a melody moving in time.

name: Steps and skips
explanation: A step moves to the very next note name (C→D). A skip jumps over one (C→E). Melodies mostly step; chords are built from skips.

questions.promptText: C up to D is a…
questions.explanation: Next-door note names are steps.
choiceExplanations: Right — C and D are next-door names: a step.
A skip would pass over D and land on E.
A leap is even bigger — a fourth or more.
A repeat would stay on C.

questions.promptText: C up to E (jumping over D) is a…
questions.explanation: Skipping one letter name = a skip.
choiceExplanations: A step would land on the very next name, D.
Right — jumping over one letter (D) makes C-to-E a skip.
An octave is C to the NEXT C — eight names away.
A repeat stays put — this clearly moved.

questions.promptText: Chords like C-E-G are stacks of…
questions.explanation: Triads skip every other note — that is why they look like snowmen on the staff.
choiceExplanations: Stacked steps (C-D-E) would clash — that's a tone cluster, not a chord.
Right — triads stack skips: C skips to E skips to G. That's the snowman shape.
Stacked octaves would all share one name — no harmony in it.
Bar lines are time markers — they can't be stacked into sound.

questions.promptText: E down to D is a…
questions.explanation: One letter down, next-door key — a downward step.
choiceExplanations: Right — one letter down to the next-door key: a downward step.
A skip down from E would pass D and land on C.
Up is the wrong direction — E to D falls.
A repeat would stay on E.

questions.promptText: Most of the Ode to Joy melody moves by…
questions.explanation: It walks to its neighbors — that is what made it your perfect first song.
choiceExplanations: Skips appear only a few times — listen to how it strolls, not jumps.
Right — Ode to Joy walks to neighboring notes almost the whole way. That's why it was your perfect first song.
Octave jumps would sound like huge leaps — there are none.
There's barely a rest in it — the melody keeps walking.

name: Tier 3 check: moves, positions, subdivisions
explanation: Steps vs skips, the three home positions, and splitting the beat.

questions.promptText: F up to A (jumping G) is a…
questions.explanation: One letter skipped = a skip.
choiceExplanations: A step would land on G, the very next letter.
Right — F to A jumps over G: a skip.
A repeat stays on F.
An octave would be F to the next F — eight names up.

questions.promptText: Two even notes per beat are called…
questions.explanation: Eighths split the beat: count "1-and".
choiceExplanations: Quarter notes ARE the beat here — one per beat, not two.
Right — eighth notes split each beat in two: count '1-and'.
Half notes stretch across TWO beats — the opposite direction.
Whole notes fill four beats — far too long.

questions.promptText: How do you count four beats filled with eighth notes?
questions.explanation: Each beat gets an "and" for its second half.
choiceExplanations: '1 2 3 4' only counts the beats themselves — the halves go missing.
Right — each beat gets its 'and': eight even eighth notes.
'ONE two three' is 3/4 counting — wrong meter entirely.
'1 and a 2 and a' counts triplets — three per beat, not two.

questions.promptText: The five-finger position starting on F uses which black key?
questions.explanation: F-G-A-B♭-C — finger 4 rides the black key.
choiceExplanations: F# belongs to the G-side world — not in the F five-finger shape.
Right — F-G-A-B♭-C: finger 4 rides the black key B♭.
E♭ lives in flat keys further afield — not needed here.
There IS one — B♭ is what makes the F position feel different from C's.

questions.promptText: Moving the same five-finger shape from C to G is called a…
questions.explanation: Same shape, new home — that is the pentascale shift.
choiceExplanations: Right — same shape, new home key. That's the pentascale shift (a transposition of position).
A chord change swaps harmonies INSIDE one position — this moves the whole hand.
A cadence is how a phrase ENDS — nothing to do with hand position.
A turnaround is the little progression that loops a song back to the top.

questions.promptText: A quick two-note lead-in before a downbeat (like Susanna) is a…
questions.explanation: Pickup notes launch the phrase into beat one.
choiceExplanations: Right — quick lead-in notes before the downbeat are a pickup. Susanna opens with one.
A fill decorates a GAP between phrases — usually at the end, not the start.
A turnaround steers the harmony back to the top of the form.
A rest is silence — a pickup is the opposite: notes arriving early.

name: The 1-3-5 recipe
explanation: A major triad stacks the 1st, 3rd, and 5th notes of its scale: C-E-G, F-A-C, G-B-D. Same recipe, any root.

questions.promptText: A major triad is built from scale degrees…
questions.explanation: Root, third, fifth — the triad recipe.
choiceExplanations: 1-2-3 are neighbors — played together they clash instead of ringing.
Right — root, third, fifth: 1-3-5 is the triad recipe.
1-4-5 skips the third — that's a sus4 sound, hollow and unresolved.
1-5-8 is a bare octave-and-fifth power chord — no third, no major/minor color.

questions.promptText: The notes of C major are…
choiceExplanations: C-D-E is three steps in a row — a scale fragment, not a chord.
Right — C(1), E(3), G(5): the C major triad.
C-F-G stacks the wrong intervals — F isn't C's third.
C-E-A re-roots the sound on A — that's an A minor shape, not C major.

questions.promptText: The notes of G major are…
choiceExplanations: G-A-B is a scale walk — steps, not stacked skips.
Right — G(1), B(3), D(5): the G major triad.
G-C-E is actually C major flipped over — C's family, not G's.
G-B-E re-roots on E — an E minor shape in disguise.

questions.promptText: The notes of F major are…
choiceExplanations: Right — F(1), A(3), C(5): the F major triad.
F-G-A is three neighbors — a cluster of steps, not a triad.
F-B♭-C skips the third — a sus4 color, not major.
F-A-D re-roots on D — that's a D minor shape.

questions.promptText: Playing E-G-C (the same three notes, re-ordered) gives you…
questions.explanation: Same pitch family = same chord, just re-stacked — an inversion.
choiceExplanations: Same three pitch names can only be the same chord family.
Right — same pitch family, re-stacked: C major in inversion.
A scale is notes in a row — this is still a stack of three.
Nothing's wrong — inversions are how real accompaniments move smoothly.

name: I, IV, and V — the primary chords
explanation: In any key, the chords built on degrees 1, 4, and 5 are the primary chords. In C: C (I), F (IV), G or G7 (V). V7 pulls home to I.

questions.promptText: In the key of C, chord I is…
questions.explanation: The chord built on the key note is I — home.
choiceExplanations: Right — the chord built on the key note is I: home.
F is IV in this key — the 'away' chord.
G is V — the tension chord that leans home.
Am is vi — a relative, but not home base.

questions.promptText: In the key of C, chord IV is…
questions.explanation: Count up four: C-D-E-F. IV is F.
choiceExplanations: D is degree 2 — that chord would be ii.
E is degree 3 — iii territory.
Right — count up four (C-D-E-F): IV is F.
G is degree five — that's V, one further along.

questions.promptText: In the key of C, chord V is…
questions.explanation: Count up five: C-D-E-F-G. V is G.
choiceExplanations: F is degree four — IV, not V.
Right — count up five (C-D-E-F-G): V is G.
A is degree six — the vi chord.
B is degree seven — the rare, unstable vii°.

questions.promptText: Which chord most strongly pulls BACK to home?
questions.explanation: The dominant seventh leans hard toward I — that pull ends most phrases.
choiceExplanations: I IS home — there's nothing to pull back to.
IV drifts away gently but doesn't demand a return.
Right — V7 leans hardest toward I; that pull closes most phrases.
They don't all rest — V7 in particular practically points at the exit.

questions.promptText: Why do musicians name chords by NUMBER instead of letter?
questions.explanation: I-IV-V describes the same relationships in any key — the Nashville idea you'll meet later.
choiceExplanations: Length isn't the point — 'IV' and 'F' are both short.
Right — I-IV-V names the same relationships in ANY key. That's the Nashville idea you'll meet later.
Letters aren't old-fashioned — they're just tied to one key at a time.
They do — number-talk is how working musicians move songs between keys on the spot.

name: Waltz time — 3/4
explanation: 3/4 has three quarter-note beats per bar: ONE-two-three. Amazing Grace, Home on the Range, and every waltz live here.

questions.promptText: How many beats fit in one bar of 3/4?
questions.explanation: Three quarter-note beats per bar.
choiceExplanations: Two per bar is 2/4 — the march.
Right — the top 3 means three quarter-note beats per bar.
Four per bar is 4/4 — common time.
Six per bar would be 6/8's count — a compound lilt.

questions.promptText: You hear: ONE-two-three, ONE-two-three. The meter is…
questions.explanation: An accent every three beats — the waltz.
choiceExplanations: 2/4 accents every TWO beats — too square for this sway.
Right — an accent every three beats is 3/4: the waltz.
4/4 would add a fourth count before the accent returns.
12/8 is a long rolling shuffle bar — four groups of three.

questions.promptText: Which note value fills an ENTIRE bar of 3/4?
questions.explanation: A dotted half lasts three beats — one full waltz bar.
choiceExplanations: A half note is two beats — one beat short of the bar.
Right — a dotted half lasts three beats: one full waltz bar.
A whole note is four beats — it overflows 3/4 by one.
A quarter note fills just one beat of the three.

questions.promptText: A 3/4 bar holds a half note so far. What completes it?
questions.explanation: Two beats used, one left.
choiceExplanations: Right — the half note used two beats; one quarter note completes the three.
Another half note would push the bar to four beats — overfull.
A whole note alone outlasts the entire bar.
Not full yet — beat three is still waiting.

questions.promptText: The strongest beat in a 3/4 bar is…
questions.explanation: ONE-two-three: the downbeat carries the sway.
choiceExplanations: Right — ONE-two-three: the downbeat carries the waltz's sway.
Beat 2 is a light middle beat.
Beat 3 lifts you INTO the next downbeat — it's the springboard, not the landing.
They aren't equal — without a strong ONE there'd be no sway at all.

name: Tier 4 check: chords and meters
explanation: Triad recipes, the primary-chord family, hearing the dominant lean, and 3/4 vs 4/4.

questions.promptText: The 1-3-5 of F major is…
questions.explanation: F, A, C.
choiceExplanations: Right — F, A, C: root, third, fifth of F major.
F-G-C has a second (G) where the third should be — a sus2 color.
F-B-D drifts into B-diminished territory — not F's notes.
F-A-D re-roots on D — a D minor shape.

questions.promptText: In C, the three primary chords are…
questions.explanation: I, IV, V = C, F, G.
choiceExplanations: Dm and Em are the ii and iii chords — cousins, not the primaries.
Right — I, IV, V in C is C, F, G.
C-E-G are the notes of ONE chord, not three different chords.
F, G, Am leaves out home itself — I must be in the set.

questions.promptText: The chord that sounds like it is LEANING toward home is…
questions.explanation: The dominant seventh asks; I answers.
choiceExplanations: I IS home — it answers, it doesn't lean.
IV wanders away but sits comfortably where it lands.
Right — V7 leans toward home; the dominant seventh asks and I answers.
vi is a soft substitute for home — no pull in it.

questions.promptText: ONE-two-three, ONE-two-three is…
questions.explanation: Waltz time.
choiceExplanations: 2/4 counts in twos — ONE-two.
Right — ONE-two-three is 3/4: waltz time.
4/4 counts in fours.
There's a clear repeating count of three — that's very much a meter.

questions.promptText: G7 adds which note to the G triad?
questions.explanation: G-B-D plus F — the seventh gives it the pull.
choiceExplanations: E isn't in the G7 stack — that would suggest an Em color.
Right — G-B-D plus F: the added seventh gives G7 its pull.
A would make it a G6 flavor — sweet, but no tension.
C is where G7 WANTS to go, not a note inside it.

questions.promptText: Changing chords WITHOUT breaking the pulse matters because…
questions.explanation: Listeners forgive a wrong note; they feel a broken pulse.
choiceExplanations: Looks have nothing to do with it — grooves are heard and felt.
Right — the groove IS the song. Listeners forgive a wrong note; they feel a broken pulse.
Chords are the harmony — hardly optional, but the POINT is keeping time through them.
Speed isn't the goal — steadiness through the change is.

name: Scale degrees: the number map
explanation: The C major scale is C-D-E-F-G-A-B, numbered 1-7. Degrees, not letters, are how musicians think — numbers transpose.

questions.promptText: In C major, degree 5 is…
choiceExplanations: E is degree 3.
F is degree 4.
Right — count C(1) D(2) E(3) F(4) G(5): G is degree 5.
A is degree 6.

questions.promptText: In C major, degree 3 is…
questions.explanation: C-D-E: E is 3.
choiceExplanations: D is degree 2 — one short.
Right — C-D-E: E is degree 3.
F is degree 4 — one past it.
G is degree 5.

questions.promptText: The C major scale uses…
questions.explanation: C major is the all-white-key scale — that is why we start here.
choiceExplanations: Right — C major is the all-white-key scale. That's exactly why we start here.
One black key describes F major (B♭) or G major (F#) — not C.
Two black keys arrives with keys like D major — later tiers.
All black keys isn't any major scale — though it IS a pentatonic party trick.

questions.promptText: Where does the right-hand thumb tuck happen in a one-octave C scale?
questions.explanation: Fingers 1-2-3, thumb slips under, then 1-2-3-4-5 to the top.
choiceExplanations: After finger 2 is too soon — you'd run out of fingers by the top.
Right — 1-2-3, thumb tucks under, then 1-2-3-4-5 carries you to the top.
After finger 4 is too late — the tuck happens mid-scale, not near the end.
Without a tuck, five fingers can't cover eight notes.

questions.promptText: The major triad on C uses degrees…
questions.explanation: Chords and scales are the same map — the triad picks 1, 3, and 5.
choiceExplanations: 1-2-3 are neighbors — a cluster, not a chord.
Right — the triad picks degrees 1, 3, and 5. Chords and scales are one map.
2-4-6 builds the ii chord (D minor in C) — a different family.
5-6-7 is another run of neighbors — steps, not a stack of skips.

name: Reading chord symbols
explanation: A letter above the music names a major chord: C means C-E-G. A "7" adds the seventh (G7), "m" makes it minor.

questions.promptText: The symbol "C" above the staff means play…
questions.explanation: A bare letter = that major triad.
choiceExplanations: A single note would just be written in the music — symbols speak in chords.
Right — a bare letter means that major triad: C = C-E-G.
Minor gets a lowercase m: 'Cm'.
Scales never appear as chord symbols — symbols are harmony shorthand.

questions.promptText: The symbol "G7" means…
questions.explanation: The 7 adds F on top of G-B-D — the leaning chord.
choiceExplanations: Plain G major would be just the letter 'G'.
G minor would be written 'Gm'.
Right — G7 is the dominant seventh: G-B-D plus F, the leaning chord.
The 7 names an added NOTE (the seventh), not a count of Gs.

questions.promptText: The symbol "Dm" means…
questions.explanation: A small m = minor.
choiceExplanations: D major would be a bare 'D'.
Right — the small m means minor: D-F-A.
Dominant would be written 'D7'.
Diminished gets 'dim' or the ° symbol.

questions.promptText: Chord symbols mainly help you…
choices: Grasp the harmony at a glance
questions.explanation: Symbols are the fastest map of a song — the notation these genres run on.
choiceExplanations: Reading every note is what staff notation does — symbols zoom OUT.
Right — symbols hand you the harmony at a glance. Blues, gospel, and country run on them.
No shortcut skips practicing — symbols just aim it better.
Bar counting is what the chart layout shows — symbols carry the harmony.

questions.promptText: A bar shows the symbol F. Your left hand's most useful single note is…
questions.explanation: The root anchors the chord — bass players live on roots.
choiceExplanations: Right — the root anchors the chord. Bass players live on roots.
A is the third — pretty, but it floats without the root under it.
C is the fifth — supportive, but not the anchor.
It matters a lot — the root tells everyone what the chord IS.

name: Finished or asking?
explanation: Phrases end with punctuation: landing on I sounds finished (a period); pausing on V sounds like a question waiting for an answer.

questions.promptText: A phrase that ends on chord I sounds…
questions.explanation: Home is where phrases rest — a full stop.
choiceExplanations: Unfinished is how V feels — I is the opposite.
Right — ending on I sounds finished, at rest. Home is a full stop.
There's nothing wrong about it — it's the most natural ending in music.
Volume doesn't change with harmony — loudness is a separate choice.

questions.promptText: A phrase that pauses on V or V7 sounds…
questions.explanation: The dominant leaves the sentence hanging — the next phrase answers.
choiceExplanations: Finished is how landing on I feels — V refuses to settle.
Right — pausing on V or V7 sounds like a question; the next phrase answers it.
An ending on V would leave every listener hanging — try it!
The music keeps sounding — 'silent' isn't a harmonic feeling.

questions.promptText: Amazing Grace's halfway point parks on G7. That phrase is…
questions.explanation: The hymn breathes at the dominant, then the second half brings it home.
choiceExplanations: Complete phrases land on I — this one deliberately doesn't.
Right — the hymn breathes at the dominant (a question), then the second half brings it home.
No key change happens — G7 still belongs to C's world.
It's a 300-year-old design, not a mistake — tension that makes the return sweeter.

questions.promptText: The very last chord of most songs in C is…
questions.explanation: Endings land at home.
choiceExplanations: F (IV) drifts away — a strange place to stop.
G7 (V7) would end the song mid-sentence — pure suspense.
Right — songs in C come home to C. Endings land at rest.
Am is a shadow-home — moody, but not the resting place these songs choose.

questions.promptText: Hearing where a phrase is heading helps you…
questions.explanation: Phrasing is the difference between typing notes and telling a story.
choiceExplanations: Louder isn't a plan — dynamics follow the phrase, not the other way around.
Right — hearing where a phrase heads lets you breathe and shape it. That's the difference between typing notes and telling a story.
Skipping the ending skips the payoff the whole phrase was building.
Reading speed is a separate skill — phrasing is about meaning, not pace.

name: Tier 5 check: degrees, symbols, cadences, waltz
explanation: Everything Arc I taught, meeting in one place.

questions.promptText: In C major, degree 4 is…
questions.explanation: C-D-E-F: F is 4.
choiceExplanations: E is degree 3.
Right — C-D-E-F: F is degree 4.
G is degree 5.
B is degree 7.

questions.promptText: "G7" tells you to play…
questions.explanation: Triad plus the seventh.
choiceExplanations: G-B-D is plain G major — the 7 asks for one more note.
Right — G7 is the triad plus the seventh: G-B-D-F.
G-C-E is C major flipped over — different chord entirely.
One lone G is just a note — symbols always mean chords.

questions.promptText: A dotted half note in 3/4 lasts…
questions.explanation: Three beats = one waltz bar.
choiceExplanations: One beat is a plain quarter note.
Two beats is an undotted half note — the dot adds half again.
Right — dotted half = three beats = one full 3/4 bar.
Two bars would need six beats — twice what the dotted half holds.

questions.promptText: A phrase pausing on the dominant sounds…
questions.explanation: V asks; I answers.
choiceExplanations: Finished is the sound of landing on I.
Right — pausing on the dominant sounds like a question. V asks; I answers.
Minor is a chord QUALITY — this is about where the phrase rests.
Time keeps flowing — harmony can't knock you out of meter.

questions.promptText: The primary chords of C major are…
questions.explanation: I, IV, and V.
choiceExplanations: Right — I, IV, and V: C, F, and G.
Dm is the ii chord — a cousin, not a primary.
E and Am are iii and vi — the minor relatives.
This set is missing home — C itself must be in it.

questions.promptText: The C major scale's thumb tuck comes after finger…
choiceExplanations: After 2 is too early — you'd arrive at the top a finger short.
Right — 1-2-3, tuck, then 1-2-3-4-5 to the top.
After 4 is too late for a smooth crossing.
Finger 5 caps the scale at the very top — no tucking after it.

questions.promptText: Why did every scale lesson end in a riff or fill?
choices: Scales exist to make music, not laps
questions.explanation: A scale is a toolbox, not a lap around the track.
choiceExplanations: Not tradition — intention. Laps for their own sake teach laps.
Right — scales exist to make music. The riff or fill is the point of the ladder.
Filling time is exactly what those lessons refused to do.
It did — every scale lesson ended by turning the scale into music.

questions.promptText: Melody in the right hand, roots in the left, at tempo, no help — that is the definition of…
questions.explanation: Accurate, in time, unassisted: the standard every tier boss asks for.
choiceExplanations: Practice is how you GET there — this describes the arrival.
Right — accurate, in time, unassisted: performance mastery, the standard every tier boss asks for.
Sight-reading is playing something NEW from notation — this song you know well.
Improvisation invents in the moment — this is delivering a known piece cleanly.
